source.title: Corrupting Neuron Explanations of Deep Visual Features
source.authors: Divyansh Srivastava; Tuomas P. Oikarinen; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how probing-data corruption changes neuron explanations, but it does not test whether neurons naturally respond to unrelated inputs or whether neurons are polysemantic under any listed version.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern deliberately corrupted probing datasets and changes to assigned neuron concepts or descriptions. They do not measure polysemanticity or spontaneous neuron responses. The corruptions are induced interventions, not evidence that the networks naturally exhibit mixed responses. The paper also reports results for other layers, MILAN on ResNet50, targeted MILAN corruption, and other corruption conditions; these are not included in the rows below.
record.test_reason: The study measures how Network Dissection and MILAN neuron labels change when the probing data is deliberately corrupted, using Gaussian, uniform or Bernoulli noise and PGD perturbations, on VGG16-Places365 and ResNet50-ImageNet. It never measures whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. It does not mention polysemanticity or superposition. No version is tested. Label instability under induced corruption is a different construct from polysemanticity or from how explanations are scored on clean data (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that neuron explanation methods are not robust to random noise or designed perturbations of probing data, and that top-layer units with higher-level concepts are easier to manipulate.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates robustness of Network Dissection and MILAN explanations to corruptions of their probing data rather than applying the original work's neuron-identification measurement to test polysemanticity.
record.method_sensitivity: Explanation changes vary with perturbation magnitude, layer, corruption method, and fraction of probing images corrupted; the authors report greater susceptibility in higher layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Concepts assigned by Network Dissection and descriptions from MILAN change for many units under small random noise. Designed perturbations of under 10% of probing images change the concepts of more than 80% of higher-layer units. Higher layers and higher-level concept categories are more susceptible.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron explanation labels are not robust to corruption of the probing dataset, especially in deeper layers.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The experiments deliberately corrupt probing data and therefore do not establish natural polysemanticity. The selected quantitative rows cover only the deepest listed layers and some reported conditions; many additional layer and method results are left out.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other Network Dissection layers and the remaining reported settings, including MILAN results beyond the VGG16-Places365 conv5 3 Gaussian-noise entries, from Tables 1–3 and Appendix Tables A.1–A.7; also omitted figure-only corruption comparisons and the validation-accuracy plot. These are omitted to keep the record focused on representative numeric probing-corruption outcomes.

untested.parts: Whether vision-model neurons naturally respond to several unrelated inputs; not measured.
Superposition as a cause; not studied.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure; not studied.
Effects of architecture, activation function or training on the polysemantic share. The adversarially trained ResNet50 result concerns attack robustness, not polysemanticity.
Whether mixed responses reduce to a single feature; not studied.
Dependence of polysemantic counts on activation range or explanation scoring. The study varies probing data, not the measure of polysemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: r9–r11 carry ResNet50 layer3 untargeted values in place of the VGG16 conv5_3 targeted values. The remaining rows match Tables 1–2. No result bears on any polysemanticity version, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision-model neurons naturally respond strongly to several unrelated inputs.
Language-model neuron polysemanticity and layer differences.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemanticity and performance.
Whether apparent mixed responses resolve into a shared feature or related jobs.
Whether polysemanticity counts depend on activation range or explanation scoring; the study varies probing data but does not measure polysemanticity.

rows.subject: VGG16-Places365
rows.operation_detail: Added Gaussian random noise to the probing dataset and compared clean and manipulated MILAN descriptions.
rows.measure: Mean F1-BERT score between clean and manipulated descriptions
rows.baseline: Clean descriptions; F1-BERT maximum for similar strings is 1.0
rows.note: A lower score indicates more dissimilar descriptions; this measures explanation change under corruption, not polysemanticity.
